sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte latin de zoo84/1l.xml (Physiologus Latinus X / Versio C, edition Gebert 2010, "Der Satyr im Bad", Mittellateinisches Jahrbuch 45), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. 24 chapitres correspondant exactement au decoupage du temoin latin (memes xml:id). Les passages marques [...] correspondent a des lacunes du manuscrit non completees dans l'edition source.

div.head: The Lion
div.p: The lion is the king of all animals and beasts.
Therefore Jacob too, blessing Judah, said: ‘Judah is a lion’s whelp, my son,’ and so forth.
The Physiologus relates of the lion that it has three natures.
The first nature of the lion is this:

when it walks and makes its way into the mountains, the scent of hunters comes to it; and with its tail it covers its tracks, so that the hunters may not follow its tracks and find its den and seize it.

So too my Savior, understood as a lion, conquering, of the tribe of Judah, the root of David — sent by the everlasting Father — covered his intelligible tracks, that is, his divinity, becoming with the angels an angel, with the thrones a throne, with the powers a power, until he descended into the womb of his mother Mary, that he might save the human race that had gone astray; and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. And this not knowing, all those who saw him descending said: ‘Who is this King of glory?’
The second nature of the lion is this:
when it sleeps, it keeps watch; its eyes are open.
In the Song of Songs it is testified, saying: ‘I sleep, but my heart watches.’ For he who keeps Israel shall neither sleep nor slumber.
The third nature of the lion is this:
when the lioness has given birth to her cub dead, she guards her offspring until, on the third day, its father comes and breathes upon its face, and raises it up.
So too the almighty Father of all raised on the third day from the dead the Lord Jesus Christ, the firstborn of all creation. Well did Jacob say: ‘A lion’s whelp’ — he who raised him up.

div.head: The Lizard
div.p: There is a creature called the lizard. The Physiologus said: when it grows old, it is hindered in both eyes and becomes blind, and does not see the light of the sun. What then does it do for its own nature? It seeks out a wall, entering into a crack of the wall, facing toward the east; and at the rising of the sun its eyes are opened.

Lest the eyes of your heart ever be hindered, seek then him who makes the sun of righteousness rise, the Lord Jesus Christ, whose name is called the Dayspring by the prophet; and this sun of righteousness will open for you the intelligible eyes of your heart.

div.head: The Caladrius
div.p: As it is written in Deuteronomy, the Physiologus relates of it that it is entirely white, having no black part. Its inward parts cure the dimness of clouded eyes, and it is found even in the courts of kings. And if anyone is sick, it is known from the caladrius whether he will live or die. If the man’s sickness is unto death, the caladrius turns its face away, and all know that he will die. But if the man’s sickness is unto life, the caladrius looks upon him, and the sick man upon the caladrius, and it draws in the man’s sickness and scatters it away, and the sick man will be healed.

This caladrius bears the good person of the Savior. For our Lord is entirely white, having not one particle of blackness. For it is said that the prince of this world came and found nothing in him. Coming from the heights of the holy heavens, he turned his divinity away from the Jews; but coming to the Gentiles, taking away from us our sicknesses, he bore our weaknesses. He was lifted up upon the wood of the cross. Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men.
Well, then, has the Physiologus discoursed of the caladrius.

But tell me, since the caladrius is an unclean bird, how is it brought forward in the person of Christ? The serpent too is unclean. John says that as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so it is fitting that the Son of Man be lifted up. It is the more prudent for it, for it is a double creature, both praiseworthy and blameworthy.

div.head: The Pelican
div.p: Well does David say: ‘I have become like the pelican in the wilderness, and like the night-raven in the house.’

The Physiologus relates of the pelican that it is exceedingly fond of its young. But if it has borne offspring, and they have grown, they strike their parents in the face. The parents then strike them and kill them. Then, in mercy, the parents mourn their young for three days, whom they had killed. On the third day their father comes and tears open his own side, and his blood drips upon the dead bodies of the chicks, and by that same blood he raises them from the dead.

So too our Lord says through Isaiah: ‘I have begotten and exalted children, but they have despised me.’ Our Maker begot us, and we struck him. How did we strike him? We served the creature more than the Creator. But coming to the height of the cross, our Savior opened and tore his side, and his blood dripped for our salvation, for eternal life. Blood, because it is said: ‘Taking the cup, he blessed it.’ And water, for the baptism of repentance.
Well has the Physiologus discoursed of the pelican.

div.head: The Night-Raven
div.p: The Physiologus said: it is a bird that loves the night more than the day.

Our Lord Jesus Christ loved us, who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death — the people of the Gentiles above the people of the Jews. For they had then the adoption and the promise of the fathers; therefore the Savior says: ‘Fear not, little flock.’ In this alone was God well pleased with him.
But tell me, since the night-raven is unclean according to the Law — therefore the apostle says of the Savior that he knew no sin, he did no sin, and he humbled himself that he might exalt us.
Well, then, does the Physiologus relate of the night-raven.

div.head: The Eagle
div.p: David says: ‘Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.’

The Physiologus said of the eagle that if it grows old, its wings become heavy and its eyes grow dim. What then does it do? It seeks a fountain of clean water, and flies up into the air of the sun, spreads its wings, and descends into the fountain of water. It is baptized three times, and rises, casting off the dimness of its eyes, and is renewed and made new.

So too you, having an old garment, and your eyes grown dim, seek the spiritual fountain, the Word of God, who said: ‘They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.’ And flying up to the height of the sun of righteousness, Jesus Christ, he himself will strip from you the old garment of the devil, and will baptize you in the everlasting fountain, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This, then, is what David says: ‘Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.’

div.head: The Hoopoe
div.p: Well is it written: ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.’ And how are there those who kill father or mother?

There is a bird called in Latin the hoopoe, whose young, if they see their parents growing old, pluck out their parents’ old feathers, and lick their eyes, and warm their parents, and they become new again.
How is it, then, that unreasoning men do not love their parents?
Well has the Physiologus discoursed of the hoopoe.

div.head: The Viper
div.p: Well did John say to the Pharisees: ‘Offspring of vipers, who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?’

The Physiologus tells of the viper that it has the face of a man, and of a woman down to the navel, and down to the tail it has the shape of a crocodile. The female has no passage in her sex, but only, as it were, the eye of a needle. And if the male mates with the female, he pours his seed into the female’s mouth; and if the female drinks the seed, she bites off the male’s members, and the male dies at once. But when the young have grown, they eat through their mother’s belly, and so come forth, having killed both father and mother.

Well, then, did John liken the Pharisees to the viper, since as the viper kills its father or mother, so the Pharisees killed their wisest parents — the prophets — and our Savior Jesus Christ, and the Church. How then shall they flee the wrath to come, since the father and the mother live forever, but they themselves are dead?

div.head: The Serpent
div.p: The Lord says in the gospel: ‘Be wise, therefore, as serpents, and simple as doves.’
Well does the Physiologus relate of it that the serpent has four natures.
This is a nature of the serpent.

When it grows old, its eyes grow dim; and if it wishes to become young again, it abstains from food and fasts forty days and nights, until its skin is loosened; then it seeks out a rock, or a narrow crevice, and forces itself to pass through it, and so afflicts its body and puts off its old age, and becomes new again.

So too man, if he takes up this most prudent example of the serpent, and wishes to put off the old age of the world through the narrow and afflicted gate, let him hasten first to afflict his body with fasting. For narrow is the way, and afflicted, that leads to eternal life.
On the third nature of the serpent.
When it comes to drink water from a spring, it does not bring its venom with it, but leaves it behind in its den, or in its lair.

We too, who hasten to the everlasting water, full of divine and heavenly words, in the church, ought not to bring with us the venom of malice — that is, polluted desires — but to come forward in the most perfect purity.
On the fourth nature of the serpent.
When a man comes and wishes to kill it, it gives up its whole body, but guards its head.
We too, in the time of temptation, ought to give up our whole body, but guard our head — that is, not deny Christ, as the holy martyrs did; for Christ is the head of all.

div.head: The Ant
div.p: On the nature of the ant.

When it stores up wheat in the earth, it divides its grains into two parts, lest perchance the winter should overtake it, and the rain, soaking in, should make the grains sprout, and it should perish of hunger.

And you too, turn the words of the Old Testament to spiritual understanding, lest the letter kill. Paul said that the law is spiritual. For the Jews, attending only to the flesh, perished of hunger, and became the murderers of the prophets.
On the second nature of the ant.

Often it goes into the field and climbs up an ear of grain at harvest time, and takes down its grains; but before it climbs up, it smells the ear from below, and by the smell knows well whether it is wheat or barley. If it is barley, it lets it go and moves on to wheat. For barley is the food of beasts, and it takes the wheat, because it is stored in the granary.
Barley, then, shall be likened to strange doctrine; wheat, to the equity of the faith of the Spirit.
[Cf. Ambrose, Hexameron 6.4.16] On the little ant.

For the ant dares more than its strength; nor is it compelled by servitude to labor, but by its own foresight and forethought it lays up beforehand supplies of food for the future — whose diligence Scripture bids you imitate, saying: ‘Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and be wiser than she.’ For she possesses no cultivated field, has no one to compel her, nor labors under a master; yet see how she prepares food, storing up for herself a harvest from your own labors. And though you often are in want, she is not in need. No granaries are shut to her, no guard is impenetrable, no heap inviolable; the watchman looks on and dares not forbid the theft. The owner sees his loss and takes no vengeance; in a black column the plunder is carried off, the paths swarm across the fields with the company of travelers; and what cannot be grasped in her narrow mouth, great grains of corn are dragged along upon her shoulders. The master of the harvest waits, and is ashamed to grudge such small gains to so pious an industry.

div.head: The Sirens and Onocentaur
div.p: The prophet Isaiah spoke thus: that sirens and onocentaurs and hedgehogs shall dance there.

The Physiologus said this: that sirens are deadly, and in the sea they cry out with various voices, so that sailors, when they hear them, are led astray. From the head to the navel they have the form of a man, and downward, to the tail, they are winged. Likewise the onocentaur: part of its body is that of a man, but the other part has the likeness of an ass.

To these, then, are compared double-hearted men, who take on the appearance of piety while having the character of adversaries and heretics. For by their most sweet words, like sirens, they lead astray the hearts of the innocent.

div.head: The Hedgehog
div.p: The hedgehog indeed has a form entirely of spines, and is entirely full of thorns. The Physiologus says of it that at the time of the vintage it climbs up the vine over a bunch of grapes, and knocks its berries to the ground; and coming down, it rolls itself over the berries, and they cling to its spines, and it carries them to its young, leaving the cluster of the bunch empty.

And you, Christian, if you are the vine of God, keep watch, then, lest the hedgehog climb up to you — that is, the devil — lest he ever corrupt your good way and scatter it to his own offspring, that is, to idols and to the adversary powers, and leave your cluster empty. For if you keep your bunch of grapes, you may be brought to the spiritual winepress, that you may be stored in the cellar — that is, in the courts of Christ the king — which can offer good wine for the gladness of man’s heart.

div.head: The Fox
div.p: This animal is deceitful in this manner: if it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it seeks out a cleft in the earth, and throws itself down on its back, looking upward, and holds its breath within itself in every way, so that the birds think it is dead, and come down to devour it. But it suddenly rises up, and seizes and eats them.

To this the devil shall be likened, who is deceitful in all his works. Whoever, then, wishes to partake of his flesh — that is, of his deeds — dies at once. For the Savior said this of Herod, the son of the devil’s Herod: ‘Go and tell that fox.’ And in the Song of Songs: ‘Take us the foxes that destroy the vineyard’ — of which vineyard David spoke.

div.head: The Panther
div.p: The prophet says thus: ‘I have become like a panther to the house of Ephraim.’

The Physiologus testifies thus of the panther, that its nature is such that it is a friend to all animals, but an enemy to the dragon. Its appearance is many-colored, like Joseph’s coat, being entirely varied. It is a quiet and very gentle animal. When it has eaten and is satisfied, it sleeps in its den, and on the third day rises from sleep; and when it has risen and gone out from its place, it cries out with a great voice, and from its voice comes a sweetness of spices, and those who are far and those who are near, hearing its voice, follow it, so that they may be filled with its odor.

So too my Savior Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day. All who are far and who are near, as the apostle said, he filled with the sweetness of faith. He is many-colored in that he has won over the nations of the earth in many ways; he himself is the tower of strength, of peace, of mercy, and of virtue and of glory. As the Lord, he pursues the ancient dragon, the most wicked devil.
For the Scriptures have told us nothing without a likeness.

div.head: The Great Sea-Monster, the Aspidochelone
div.p: There is a sea-monster in the sea, the aspidochelone; it has two natures.
The first is this:

if it is hungry, it opens its mouth, and a very great and sweet odor comes out from its mouth, so that the smaller fish are drawn to it and follow its sweetness, and all gather together in its mouth; and when its mouth is full, it closes upon all the fish and swallows them.
But the great and mature fish do not draw near to its mouth.
On the second nature of the fish.

For it shows itself, in some small measure, like an island. Sailors think it to be an island, and after the violence of a storm, tie their ships to it; and when they have kindled a fire upon it, to cook or to warm themselves, and it feels the fire, it plunges into the depths, and drags down after it all the ships that were tied to it.

To this creature shall be likened the harlot woman, of whom Solomon says: ‘Honey drips from the lips of a harlot, who anoints her throat for a time; but afterward she is found more bitter than gall, and sharper than a two-edged sword,’ which plunges the sinner into darkness. But the perfect and the cautious do not draw near to her. Such was Joseph before the Egyptian woman; such was Elijah rebuking Jezebel; such was Susanna in the midst of the elders. Well, then, is the woman likened to this fish.

div.head: The Unicorn
div.p: In the psalm it says thus: ‘My horn shall be exalted like the horn of the unicorn.’

The Physiologus says of it that it is a small animal. It is an animal like a kid, very gentle, having one horn upon its head; and no hunter can approach it, because it has an exceedingly strong horn. Yet when it runs about leaping, it is caught in this manner: a most chaste virgin is set before it, and when it sees the virgin, at once it comes, gentle, and lays itself in her lap; and while it is being warmed, thus she carries it, hastening, into the house of the king. For no hunter is able to capture it.

So too is our Savior, of whom the prophet said: ‘He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David.’ For while he appeared in the world, no kings and no evil powers were able to do him harm, when the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.

div.head: The Stag
div.p: The Physiologus says that it is an enemy to the dragon and pursues it, wishing to kill it. When the dragon flees before it and hides itself in crevices, the stag swiftly goes to a spring and fills its belly with much water, and, coming, vomits it out after the dragon. The dragon, driven out by the water, comes forth troubled, and the stag devours it.

So too is our Lord Jesus Christ: he pursued the great dragon, the devil, even into the lower parts of the earth. And pouring out from his side blood and water, he put the dragon to flight through the washing of regeneration, and cut off the works of the devil.

div.head: The Salamander
div.p: If this creature enters into a furnace of fire, the fire is extinguished; or if it enters into a bath, the whole bath is made cold.
So it was with the bodies of the three young men, whom the fire did not harm, but rather struck their adversaries — because Christ strengthened them in the furnace by his power.

div.head: The Tree Called Peredexion
div.p: This tree is in India; its fruit is exceedingly sweet and very pleasant. Doves delight greatly in its fruit and dwell in its branches. The dragon is the enemy of the dove, and the dragon fears to come near the tree. For if the shadow of the tree falls toward the east, the dragon flees to the west; and if the shadow comes toward the west, the dragon flees to the east. And if the dove is found outside the shadow, the dragon kills it.

This tree we take to be the Savior, who is the tree of life to all who believe in him. In his shadow is every merit; and the apostle cries out, saying: ‘But far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of the Lord, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.’

div.head: The Antelope
div.p: There is an animal, exceedingly fierce, so that not even hunters can prevail against it. For it has long horns, having the shape of a saw, so that it can cut down great trees and bring them to the ground. When it grows thirsty, it comes to a river; there are slender willow branches there; and when, playing, it has crossed among them, it becomes entangled by its horns, and is held fast by the willow branches as if ensnared, and cries out, roaring, wishing to flee. And when the hunter hears it, he comes and kills it.

And you, O man, keep the two Testaments, the New and the Old, which are given to you for the salvation of your soul [...] that is, avarice, luxury, and all the pomps of the world, lest you begin to be entangled by them.

div.head: The Saw-Fish
div.p: This fish has very long fins. If it sees ships sailing on the sea, it strives to imitate them, and raises its fins, and races against the sailors. But if it runs thirty or forty furlongs, it grows weary, and folds its fins, and the waves carry it back to the place where it had been before.

The sea is the world; the ship is the holy Church, in which are the people of God; but this fish is the devil, who transforms himself as it were into an angel of light, that he may more easily deceive unwary souls.

div.head: The Elephant and the Mandrake
div.p: There is no lustful mating; when they wish to come together, they go along the river of paradise and find the mandrake, and the mandrake stirs together with the female. And the female, taking the mandrake, offers it to the male, and plays with him until he eats it. And when the male has eaten, he comes together with the female, and she conceives. When, then, the time comes for her to give birth, she enters into a pool of water, and the water rises to her udders, and she brings forth her young there, so that, swimming upon the waters, the newborn may have its mother’s offspring near at hand. But the serpent is the elephant’s enemy, because it kills it with its feet.

Now the nature of the elephant is this: if it falls down, it can no longer rise up. For when it wishes to sleep, it leans against a tree and sleeps. But the hunters, when they wish to capture it, cut the tree almost through; and when it comes to lean and sleep, it falls down together with the tree. And when it begins to cry out loudly with a great groan, and another elephant hears it, it comes to help it, but is not able to raise it up; both cry out together. And others come, and they too cannot raise it up. Then together they all cry out. Afterward a smaller elephant comes and puts its trunk under the larger one, and raises it up.
For if fire is kindled from its bones, neither dragon nor demon can prevail there.

The male and female elephants, then, we understand as the figure of Adam and Eve. For while they were in paradise, they knew no lustful mating. But when they had eaten of the forbidden tree, they were cast out of paradise, and, having transgressed, they died.

The Law of Moses came, and did not raise him up. Then the twelve prophets came, and neither did they raise him up. At last Jesus came, and humbled himself even unto death, and raised up Adam, who had fallen.

div.head: The Agate Stone
div.p: When craftsmen seek a pearl, they find it by means of an agate stone: they let it down into the sea on a thick cord. Then the agate settles upon the pearl and does not move. At once the divers follow the cord, and find the pearl. The shellfish that is in the sea is called the conch: it opens its mouth and receives the breeze, and the rays of the sun and moon together, and so conceives the pearl.

The agate stone, then, which finds the pearl, is understood as John, who showed the precious pearl, our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom he said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.’ This is the true pearl, which you, O man, if you wish to possess, sell your goods and give to the poor, and you will find it.

div.head: The Indian Stone
div.p: This stone has such a nature: it is a remedy for dropsy. If a physician-craftsman seeks out this stone, he binds it upon the dropsical man for three hours, and it draws out all the waters of the man’s affliction. Then he loosens the stone and sets it in the sun for three hours, and it pours out again, outside, all the fluids it had drawn in, and the stone becomes clean.
To this stone our Lord Jesus Christ is compared, who, like a good physician, has taken away from us all the sickness of our sins, and has drawn us to himself, driving away from us every weakness.
